Title: The Sleep Habit With An Actual Name — And 3 Foods That Help

Description:
You tell yourself "just one more video" and suddenly it's 1am — that's revenge bedtime procrastination, and a recent national survey found most American adults do it regularly. Blue light delays melatonin, and about 2 in 3 American adults don't get enough magnesium, so your nervous system stays wired even after the phone's finally down.

Three foods may help before bed: kiwi, pistachios, and warm milk. Research suggests two kiwis about an hour before bed can help you fall asleep faster and sleep longer. Pistachios naturally contain melatonin, tryptophan, and magnesium. And warm milk isn't just an old story — casein peptides formed as milk digests have a calming effect on the nervous system.

These foods won't fix bedtime procrastination on their own, but paired with a set phone cutoff time, falling asleep gets a lot easier.

platforms.title: Jujube, Tart Cherry, Walnut: Foods That May Actually Help You Sleep
platforms.meta_description: Melatonin naturally declines with age. Jujube, tart cherry, and walnuts each have real research behind them as gentle, food-based ways to support sleep.
platforms.body_html:
If you're lying awake more often than you used to, it's not just stress — melatonin production naturally declines with age, and disrupted sleep can throw cortisol out of balance, keeping your body in a wired state even when you're exhausted. Before reaching for medication, a few foods with real research behind them are worth trying first: jujube, tart cherry, and walnuts.

Jujube and its saponin compounds

Jujube has been used in traditional medicine for centuries, and modern research is starting to catch up. A 2020 randomized controlled trial found that participants taking a standardized wild jujube seed extract fell asleep about 15 minutes faster than a placebo group. The seed's saponins, including jujuboside, interact with GABA-A receptors — the same calming pathway targeted by many prescription sleep aids — which may explain the effect.

Tart cherry and its melatonin content

Tart cherry (Montmorency variety) is one of the few whole foods that naturally contains measurable melatonin. A systematic review of interventional studies found that regular tart cherry juice intake improved sleep duration, efficiency, or onset time in several trials. One caveat worth knowing: even concentrated tart cherry juice provides only around 85 micrograms of melatonin, far less than a typical 3–5 milligram supplement — researchers believe the benefit comes from a combination of melatonin and other plant compounds working together, not melatonin alone.

Walnuts and the magnesium-GABA connection

A 2025 randomized controlled trial had 76 young adults eat a 40-gram handful of walnuts with dinner for eight weeks; participants reported shorter time to fall asleep, better sleep efficiency, and less daytime sleepiness. Walnuts contain tryptophan, plant-based melatonin, and magnesium — and magnesium plays a direct role in maintaining healthy GABA levels, the neurotransmitter that helps quiet the nervous system at night.

How to actually use this

  • Jujube as tea, 1–2 hours before bed — dried jujube steeped in hot water is the most common way to take it.
  • Tart cherry juice or concentrate, consistently — the research used it daily for at least a week before seeing effects, so it's not a one-off fix.
  • A handful of walnuts (about 40g) with dinner — no need to overdo it; more isn't shown to help further and can sit heavy before bed.

The takeaway

None of these foods work like a sedative — they support the biological processes that already regulate your sleep, which is why consistency matters more than a single dose. Combined with a steady sleep and wake schedule, jujube, tart cherry, and walnuts are a reasonable, low-risk place to start. This article is for general information only and isn't medical advice — if insomnia persists, talk to a sleep specialist.
